credit_analysis-1.stem: Which five elements make up the 5 Cs framework for judging creditworthiness?
options: Character, capacity, capital, collateral, conditions
Cash, cost, credit, control, compliance
Customer, contract, currency, country, capital
Cost, coverage, collateral, cycle, charge
credit_analysis-1.explanation: The five elements are character (track record), capacity (ability to repay), capital (own funds), collateral (security) and conditions (loan terms and the economy).

credit_analysis-2.stem: In the 5 Cs, which element judges whether the borrower's cash flow is enough to meet repayments?
options: Capacity
Collateral
Character
Capital
credit_analysis-2.explanation: Capacity measures the borrower's ability to repay out of cash flow.

credit_analysis-3.stem: A company has cash flow available for debt service of Rp600 million and debt payments of Rp500 million a year. What is its debt service coverage ratio (DSCR)?
credit_analysis-3.explanation: DSCR = cash flow available / debt service = 600 / 500 = 1.2. A value above 1 means the cash flow is enough.

credit_analysis-4.stem: What role does collateral play in a loan decision?
options: A second source of repayment if the borrower defaults
A replacement for analysing the borrower's cash flow and income
A way to raise the interest the borrower pays
A guarantee that the borrower will never pay late
credit_analysis-4.explanation: Collateral gives the lender a back-up source of repayment, but it does not replace judging the ability to pay.

credit_analysis-5.stem: A loan agreement requires the borrower's debt-to-EBITDA ratio to stay below 3.0. What is this clause called?
options: A financial covenant
A mortgage right
A floating interest rate
A subordination clause
credit_analysis-5.explanation: A financial covenant is a limit the borrower must keep while the loan runs; a breach lets the lender act.

pph_corporate_withholding-1.stem: What is the PPh Article 23 rate on consulting fees paid to a taxpayer with an NPWP?
options: 2% of the gross amount
15% of the gross amount
5% of the gross amount
10% of the gross amount
pph_corporate_withholding-1.explanation: Technical, management and consulting services are subject to PPh 23 at 2% of the gross amount.

pph_corporate_withholding-2.stem: Which income is subject to PPh Article 23 at 15% of the gross amount?
options: Royalties for a copyright
Vehicle rental
Consulting fees
Construction services
pph_corporate_withholding-2.explanation: Dividends, interest, royalties and prizes are subject to PPh 23 at 15%; services and rent other than land and buildings are at 2%.

pph_corporate_withholding-3.stem: PT A pays Rp50,000,000 for consulting services to CV B, which has an NPWP. How much PPh 23 must PT A withhold?
pph_corporate_withholding-3.explanation: Consulting is taxed at 2%: 2% x Rp50,000,000 = Rp1,000,000.

pph_corporate_withholding-4.stem: What is the payment deadline for PPh Article 23 withheld in March?
options: The 15th of next month
The 10th of the following month
The 20th of the following month
The last day of the following month
pph_corporate_withholding-4.explanation: PPh 23 is paid by the 10th of the following month and reported by the 20th of the following month.

pph_corporate_withholding-5.stem: A non-bank company receives Rp100,000,000 of loan interest from another company that acts as a PPh 23 withholder. How much PPh 23 is withheld?
pph_corporate_withholding-5.explanation: Interest is subject to PPh 23 at 15% of the gross amount: 15% x Rp100,000,000 = Rp15,000,000.

vat_ppn_mechanics-1.stem: What is output tax for a taxable entrepreneur (PKP)?
options: VAT a PKP charges on its taxable sales
VAT the PKP pays when it buys taxable goods
Income tax on the PKP's profit
Tax paid when exporting goods
vat_ppn_mechanics-1.explanation: Output tax is the VAT a PKP charges on its supply of taxable goods or services.

options: VAT a PKP pays on its taxable purchases
VAT a PKP collects from customers
Income tax withheld from employee pay each month
A penalty for filing a return late
vat_ppn_mechanics-2.explanation: Input tax is the VAT a PKP pays on acquiring taxable goods or services.

vat_ppn_mechanics-3.stem: In one tax period a PKP has output tax of Rp80 million and creditable input tax of Rp60 million. How much VAT must it pay?
options: Rp20 million payable
Rp140 million overpaid
Rp20 million overpaid
Rp140 million payable
vat_ppn_mechanics-3.explanation: VAT payable = output tax - creditable input tax = 80 - 60 = Rp20 million.

vat_ppn_mechanics-4.stem: Which document is a formal requirement for crediting input tax?
options: A tax invoice from the supplier PKP
An ordinary receipt issued by the shop
A delivery note signed by the warehouse
A bank transfer slip with no other document
vat_ppn_mechanics-4.explanation: Input tax can be credited only with a valid tax invoice from the supplier PKP.

vat_ppn_mechanics-5.stem: Which input tax cannot be credited?
options: Tax on acquisitions not directly related to the business
Tax on raw materials used in production
Tax on services marketing the company's products
Tax on warehouse rent for storing the trade goods it sells
vat_ppn_mechanics-5.explanation: Input tax is creditable when directly related to the business; tax on unrelated acquisitions cannot be credited.

tax_dispute_audit-1.stem: To whom does a taxpayer submit an objection against a tax assessment letter?
options: The Director General of Taxes
The Tax Court in Jakarta
The head of the regional tax office
The Minister of Finance
tax_dispute_audit-1.explanation: An objection goes to the Director General of Taxes; an appeal is filed with the Tax Court only afterwards.

tax_dispute_audit-2.stem: Within what period after the assessment letter is sent must an objection be filed?
options: 3 months
1 month
6 months
12 months
tax_dispute_audit-2.explanation: An objection must be filed within 3 months of the date the assessment letter was sent.

tax_dispute_audit-3.stem: A taxpayer is unhappy with the objection decision. Where is the next legal remedy filed?
options: An appeal to the Tax Court
A second objection to the Director General
A lawsuit in the District Court
A request to the Director General through the local tax office
tax_dispute_audit-3.explanation: After the objection decision the taxpayer may appeal to the Tax Court.

tax_dispute_audit-4.stem: Within how many months of receiving the objection decision must an appeal be filed?
options: 3 months
1 month
6 months
12 months
tax_dispute_audit-4.explanation: An appeal must be filed within 3 months of receiving the objection decision.

tax_dispute_audit-5.stem: What is the longest time the Director General has to issue a decision after receiving an objection?
options: 12 months
3 months
6 months
24 months
tax_dispute_audit-5.explanation: The objection decision must be issued within 12 months of receiving the objection letter.

audit_planning_fieldwork-1.stem: What is the usual order of stages in an internal audit engagement?
options: Planning, fieldwork, reporting, follow-up
Reporting, planning, follow-up, fieldwork
Follow-up, planning, reporting, fieldwork
Fieldwork, reporting, planning, follow-up
audit_planning_fieldwork-1.explanation: An engagement runs from planning through fieldwork and reporting to follow-up of the recommendations.

audit_planning_fieldwork-2.stem: What does the auditor set during engagement planning?
options: The audit's objectives and scope
The wording of the final recommendations
Management's response to the findings
The number of findings to report
audit_planning_fieldwork-2.explanation: Planning sets the objectives, scope and approach before any evidence is collected.

audit_planning_fieldwork-3.stem: An auditor traces one transaction from start to finish to understand the process and its controls. What is this procedure called?
options: A walkthrough
A reconciliation
A confirmation
A revaluation
audit_planning_fieldwork-3.explanation: A walkthrough follows one transaction through the whole process to understand the flow and the controls.

audit_planning_fieldwork-4.stem: What must good audit evidence be?
options: Sufficient in amount and relevant and reliable
As much as possible without checking the source
Only verbal statements of the auditee
Only documents prepared by the auditee
audit_planning_fieldwork-4.explanation: Evidence must be sufficient and appropriate (relevant and reliable) to support the audit conclusion.

audit_planning_fieldwork-5.stem: When building the annual audit plan, which areas should be prioritised?
options: Those with the highest risk to the organisation's objectives
Those that are easiest to audit
Those not audited for the longest time, regardless of risk
Those the auditee asks to be reviewed leniently
audit_planning_fieldwork-5.explanation: Risk-based auditing puts the areas with the highest risk to achieving the organisation's objectives first.

options: The effect of uncertainty on objectives
The chance of a financial loss in a given year
The gap between budget and actual
A threat from outside the company
enterprise_risk_management-1.explanation: ISO 31000 defines risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives, which can be negative or positive.

enterprise_risk_management-2.stem: Which are stages of the ISO 31000 risk management process?
options: Risk assessment, risk treatment, monitoring and review
Risk identification, insurance purchase and annual audit
Hazard listing, budgeting and variance analysis
Risk register, loss reporting and claims handling
enterprise_risk_management-2.explanation: The ISO 31000 process covers communication, setting the context, risk assessment, risk treatment, and monitoring and review.

enterprise_risk_management-3.stem: A company buys insurance to cover losses from a warehouse fire. Which risk response is this?
options: Transferring the risk
Avoiding the risk
Accepting the risk
Eliminating the risk entirely
enterprise_risk_management-3.explanation: Insurance moves the financial impact of the risk to another party, which is risk transfer.

options: The risk an organisation is willing to take to meet its goals
The largest loss the organisation could absorb before it would fail
The level of risk left after all controls are applied
The probability that a given risk event will occur
enterprise_risk_management-4.explanation: Risk appetite is how much risk an organisation is willing to take on in pursuing its objectives.

enterprise_risk_management-5.stem: What is the risk that remains after a new control is applied called?
options: Residual risk
Inherent risk
Systemic risk
Cumulative risk
enterprise_risk_management-5.explanation: Residual risk is what remains after controls and treatments; inherent risk is the level before controls.

audit_reporting_followup-1.stem: What must a communication of audit results include at minimum?
options: The engagement's objectives, scope and results
A ranking of the audited units by their performance
The auditor's complete working papers and test sheets
Disciplinary actions for the staff responsible
audit_reporting_followup-1.explanation: Audit communications must cover the objectives, scope and results of the engagement.

audit_reporting_followup-2.stem: In an audit finding, what does the 'criteria' part describe?
options: The standard that should have been met
What the auditor actually found in the field
The effect the deviation has on the organisation
The fix the auditor suggests to management
audit_reporting_followup-2.explanation: Criteria is the standard that should be met; condition is what was found; cause and effect explain the gap; the recommendation is the fix.

audit_reporting_followup-3.stem: An auditor finds physical stock lower than the records. Which part of the finding explains why it happened?
options: Cause
Condition
Criteria
Effect
audit_reporting_followup-3.explanation: The cause explains why the gap happened, for example no periodic stock count.

audit_reporting_followup-4.stem: What is the purpose of follow-up after an audit report is issued?
options: To confirm the recommendations are actually carried out
To start a new audit of the same area straight after the report
To re-test every control across the organisation
To give management time to dispute the findings
audit_reporting_followup-4.explanation: Follow-up monitors whether management has implemented the recommendations or accepted the remaining risk.

audit_reporting_followup-5.stem: Management disagrees with a finding. What should the auditor do?
options: Record management's view and keep judging by the evidence
Delete the finding so the report is done sooner
Change the audit conclusion so that it matches management's view
Hold the report until management agrees
audit_reporting_followup-5.explanation: Management's response goes into the report; the finding changes only if new evidence supports it.

hris_systems-1.stem: What data does a human resource information system (HRIS) usually store and manage?
options: Employee records, leave, attendance and job history
Customer contacts, sales leads and the stage of each deal
Purchase orders, suppliers and stock levels
Ledger accounts, journals and closing entries
hris_systems-1.explanation: An HRIS keeps employee master data plus leave, attendance and employment history in one system.

hris_systems-2.stem: What is the main benefit of linking attendance data in the HRIS to payroll?
options: Less manual input, fewer pay errors
Salaries can be paid without a monthly payroll cut-off
Overtime no longer needs a supervisor's approval
Tax withholding is calculated by the bank instead
hris_systems-2.explanation: Linking attendance to payroll removes re-typing, so calculation errors fall.

hris_systems-3.stem: Why does an HRIS need role-based access?
options: So each person sees only the data their role allows
So HR staff can see every field of every employee record
So managers can log in without checking their password
So reports load faster for every user in the company
hris_systems-3.explanation: HR data is personal, so access is limited by the user's role.

hris_systems-4.stem: An employee has resigned but is still active in the HRIS. What is the most likely risk?
options: Pay still runs for someone who has left
Their leave balance keeps accruing every month
The headcount report shows one employee fewer than reality
Their tax withholding stops being calculated
hris_systems-4.explanation: A status that is not updated can make payroll keep paying someone who has left.

hris_systems-5.stem: Which is employee master data rather than transaction data?
options: Employee number and job title
Today's clock-in and clock-out times
Next week's leave request
Last month's overtime
hris_systems-5.explanation: Master data changes rarely (identity, job title); attendance, leave and overtime are repeating transaction data.

payroll_processing-1.stem: Hourly pay for overtime of a monthly-paid employee is found by dividing monthly pay by what number?

payroll_processing-2.stem: How many times the hourly wage is paid for the first overtime hour on a working day?
options: 1.5 times
1 time
2 times
3 times
payroll_processing-2.explanation: The first overtime hour is paid at 1.5 times the hourly wage, later hours at 2 times.

payroll_processing-3.stem: Monthly pay is Rp17,300,000. An employee works 3 hours of overtime on a working day. What is the overtime pay?

payroll_processing-4.stem: A permanent employee with 14 months of service is entitled to how much religious holiday allowance (THR), and when is it paid?
options: One month's wage, at the latest 7 days before the holiday
Half a month's wage, on the holiday
Two months' wages, paid in full one month before the holiday
One month's wage, a week after the holiday
payroll_processing-4.explanation: Employees with 12 months or more of service get one month's wage, paid no later than 7 days before the holiday.

payroll_processing-5.stem: An employee with 6 months of service earns Rp6,000,000 a month. What is the proportional THR?
payroll_processing-5.explanation: Proportional THR = months of service / 12 x one month's wage = 6/12 x 6,000,000 = Rp3,000,000.

labor_law_id-1.stem: Under PP 35/2021, a fixed-term contract (PKWT) based on duration can run at most how many years, including extensions?
options: 5 years
2 years
3 years
No limit
labor_law_id-1.explanation: A duration-based PKWT can run at most 5 years including extensions.

labor_law_id-2.stem: What is the longest probation period for a permanent employee (PKWTT)?
options: 3 months
1 month
6 months
12 months
labor_law_id-2.explanation: Article 60 of Law 13/2003: probation for a PKWTT is at most 3 months and must be written in the contract.

labor_law_id-3.stem: A company puts a 3-month probation in a PKWT contract. What is the legal effect?
options: The probation is void and still counts as service
It is valid because both parties agreed to it
It is valid as long as the pay is halved
The contract automatically turns into a permanent PKWTT contract
labor_law_id-3.explanation: Since the Job Creation Law, a PKWT may not include probation; if it does, the clause is void.

labor_law_id-4.stem: What does a PKWT worker receive when the contract ends normally?
options: Compensation
Severance pay
Long-service award
No entitlement at all
labor_law_id-4.explanation: A PKWT worker receives compensation money when the contract ends, not severance pay.

labor_law_id-5.stem: A permanent employee (PKWTT) is terminated for efficiency reasons. Which entitlement generally applies?
options: Severance and a long-service award, as the regulations set out
The last month's wage only, without any severance at all
The compensation money that applies to fixed-term contracts
No entitlement beyond the salary for the final month
labor_law_id-5.explanation: Severance applies to PKWTT workers on termination; the amount depends on the reason and years of service.

recruitment_selection-1.stem: The usual order of the recruitment process is...
options: Sourcing, screening, interview and assessment, verification, offer
Offer, interview and assessment, sourcing, verification, screening
Verification, offer, sourcing, screening, interview and assessment
Interview and assessment, offer, screening, sourcing, verification
recruitment_selection-1.explanation: Candidates are sourced, screened, interviewed and assessed, verified, and then given an offer.

options: Every candidate gets the same questions and is rated on the same scale
Each interviewer chooses whichever questions suit the particular candidate
The candidate leads the conversation in their own way
Questions are always kept hidden from the other interviewers
recruitment_selection-2.explanation: A structured interview uses the same questions and rating scale for every candidate so results are fair and comparable.

recruitment_selection-3.stem: What is the purpose of CV screening at the early stage?
options: To pick candidates who meet the minimum qualifications to move on
To decide the final hire before any interview takes place
To rank candidates by the salary they expect to be paid
To check references with each candidate's former employers and lecturers
recruitment_selection-3.explanation: CVs are checked against the job's minimum qualifications so only suitable candidates move on.

recruitment_selection-4.stem: What does an organisation use an Applicant Tracking System (ATS) for?
options: Tracking applicants through every hiring stage
Running employee onboarding and monthly payroll
Publishing job ads on the company's social media
Storing yearly performance appraisal results
recruitment_selection-4.explanation: An ATS stores applicant data and helps screen and track where each applicant stands in the process.

recruitment_selection-5.stem: Why are interviewer calibration sessions useful?
options: They align scoring criteria and reduce bias between interviewers
They let interviewers skip the scoring rubric for experienced candidates
They set the final salary band for each candidate
They replace the need for reference checks later on
recruitment_selection-5.explanation: Calibration aligns how interviewers score so results are more consistent and unconscious bias falls.

performance_management-1.stem: A fair performance appraisal should rate employees on what?
options: The core functions and skills of their job
The supervisor's personal impression
Length of service only
The number of hours spent in the office each week
performance_management-1.explanation: Employees should be rated on the essential functions and competencies of their job, taken from a job analysis.

options: Defining a job's duties and requirements
A ranking of employees by their output in a period
A review of an employee's past appraisal results
A survey of what employees expect from their job
performance_management-2.explanation: A job analysis records a job's duties, responsibilities and requirements, and underpins the appraisal.

options: Ratings from supervisor, peers, reports and oneself
Ratings from the direct supervisor alone
Ratings from customers and suppliers
Ratings from a written test and a structured interview
performance_management-3.explanation: 360-degree feedback gathers ratings from many angles: supervisor, peers, subordinates and self.

options: The knowledge, skills and behaviours a role needs
The list of KPIs each employee must hit this year
A description of the reporting lines in a department
The steps of the yearly performance appraisal process
performance_management-4.explanation: A competency model states the knowledge, skills and behaviours needed to succeed in a role.

performance_management-5.stem: What is the aim of performance calibration among managers?
options: To align rating standards so scores are consistent across teams
To let each manager raise the scores of their own team
To place every employee on a fixed forced-ranking curve
To replace employees' self-assessments with ratings made by managers only
performance_management-5.explanation: Calibration brings managers together to align standards so one team's scores are comparable to another's.

learning_development-1.stem: What are the four levels of training evaluation in the Kirkpatrick model?
options: Reaction, learning, behaviour, result
Cost, duration, material, instructor
Attendance, grade, certificate, bonus
Planning, execution, reporting, follow-up
learning_development-1.explanation: The four Kirkpatrick levels are reaction, learning, behaviour and results.

learning_development-2.stem: Which Kirkpatrick level do training pre-tests and post-tests measure?
options: Level 2: learning
Level 1: reaction
Level 3: behaviour
Level 4: results
learning_development-2.explanation: Level 2 measures knowledge and skills gained, for example with pre-tests and post-tests.

learning_development-3.stem: After training, three months later a supervisor observes whether participants use the new skills on the job. Which level is this?
options: Level 3: behaviour
Level 1: reaction
Level 2: learning
Level 4: results
learning_development-3.explanation: Level 3 checks whether participants apply what they learned at work, by observation or feedback.

learning_development-4.stem: Why is a training needs analysis (TNA) done before designing training?
options: To find the competency gaps to close
To choose the trainer and the training venue
To measure participants' satisfaction afterwards
To calculate the return on the training spend
learning_development-4.explanation: A TNA finds the gap between existing and required competencies so training hits the right target.

learning_development-5.stem: After a customer-service training programme, the company's complaint rate falls 20%. Which Kirkpatrick level does this show?
options: Level 4: results
Level 1: reaction
Level 2: learning
Level 3: behaviour
learning_development-5.explanation: Level 4 measures the impact of training on organisational goals, such as fewer customer complaints.

inventory_management-1.stem: In ABC inventory analysis, class A items are those that...
options: Are high-value, few in type, tightly controlled
Are low in value and make up most of the item types
Have been stored in the warehouse for the longest time
Are returned by customers most often
inventory_management-1.explanation: Class A is a few item types that account for the largest value, so they get the tightest control.

inventory_management-2.stem: What is the purpose of safety stock?
options: A buffer against demand spikes or late supply
Stock deliberately built up ahead of a seasonal promotion or holiday
The minimum order quantity that the supplier sets
Stock set aside for orders that customers have already paid for
inventory_management-2.explanation: Safety stock is extra inventory that buffers uncertain demand and supplier lead time.

inventory_management-3.stem: Annual demand is 1,000 units, ordering cost Rp50 per order, holding cost Rp10 per unit per year. What is the EOQ (square root of 2DS/H)?
options: 100 units
50 units
200 units
500 units

inventory_management-4.stem: Sales are 10 units a day, supplier lead time is 14 days, safety stock is 30 units. What is the reorder point?
options: 170 units
140 units
44 units
310 units
inventory_management-4.explanation: Reorder point = daily demand x lead time + safety stock = 10 x 14 + 30 = 170 units.

inventory_management-5.stem: Annual cost of goods sold is Rp600 million and average inventory is Rp100 million. What is inventory turnover?
options: 6 times
0.17 times
60 times
500 times
inventory_management-5.explanation: Inventory turnover = COGS / average inventory = 600 / 100 = 6 times a year.

procurement_sourcing-1.stem: The formal document a buyer sends a supplier to order goods is called a...
options: Purchase order
Tax invoice
Delivery note
Receipt
procurement_sourcing-1.explanation: A purchase order (PO) is the buyer's formal order to the supplier.

procurement_sourcing-2.stem: When is a request for quotation (RFQ) most suitable?
options: When the specification is clear and price is the main comparison
When the solution needed is not yet known and suppliers must propose one
After the goods have been received and checked
When a supplier contract is about to be terminated
procurement_sourcing-2.explanation: An RFQ asks for prices on a fixed specification; an RFP is used when suppliers are asked to propose a solution.

procurement_sourcing-3.stem: A company does not yet know which system is best and asks suppliers to propose a solution and a price. Which document is used?
options: A request for proposal (RFP)
A purchase order
A request for quotation (RFQ)
A goods receipt
procurement_sourcing-3.explanation: An RFP is used when suppliers are asked to propose a solution, not only quote a price for a fixed item.

procurement_sourcing-4.stem: Three-way matching before paying a supplier compares which three documents?
options: PO, goods receipt and supplier invoice
Quotation, signed contract and the bank transfer slip
Supplier invoice, tax report and delivery note
Approved budget, purchase order and sales report
procurement_sourcing-4.explanation: Payment is made only when the PO, the goods receipt and the supplier invoice agree.

procurement_sourcing-5.stem: Which approach is best for evaluating supplier bids?
options: Score weighted criteria: price, quality, delivery and risk
Pick the supplier offering the longest payment terms
Pick the lowest price among bids that meet the specification
Pick the supplier that the end users say they prefer
procurement_sourcing-5.explanation: A good evaluation uses weighted criteria, not price alone, because total cost includes quality and supply risk.

options: A rating of a supplier's quality, delivery and price
A checklist for registering a new supplier
A ranking of suppliers by the total value bought from each
The supplier's own assessment of its capacity
vendor_supplier_management-1.explanation: A supplier scorecard measures supplier performance regularly against agreed indicators.

vendor_supplier_management-2.stem: What is an SLA with a supplier?
options: A measurable service-level agreement, such as delivery time
A promise from the supplier to give its lowest price
A clause that lets either party end the contract early with notice
The supplier's internal quality policy statement
vendor_supplier_management-2.explanation: A service level agreement sets measurable service standards and the consequence of missing them.

vendor_supplier_management-3.stem: What is the purpose of an approved vendor list?
options: To list suppliers that passed evaluation and may be chosen
To list every supplier the company has ever paid
To rank suppliers from the lowest price upwards
To list suppliers that are still waiting for their evaluation results
vendor_supplier_management-3.explanation: Only suppliers that passed initial evaluation are listed, so purchases come from trusted sources.

vendor_supplier_management-4.stem: What is the main risk of relying on a single supplier (single sourcing)?
options: Supply stops if that supplier is disrupted
Buyers become too familiar with the supplier's staff
The company has to sign longer contracts than usual
Supplier invoices become harder to match to orders
vendor_supplier_management-4.explanation: With one supplier, a disruption there stops supply at once; a back-up supplier reduces that risk.

vendor_supplier_management-5.stem: A supplier reaches 82% OTIF against a 95% target. What is the best action?
options: Find the causes with the supplier and agree an improvement plan
Terminate the contract at once without any discussion with them
Lower the target to 82% so the supplier passes
Ignore it because the result is still above 80%
vendor_supplier_management-5.explanation: Performance below target should be analysed for causes and fixed with an agreed, monitored plan.

warehouse_logistics-1.stem: What is the main function of a warehouse management system (WMS)?
options: Managing receiving, storage and picking in a warehouse
Planning delivery routes and schedules for the company's truck fleet
Forecasting customer demand for the next quarter
Recording supplier invoices so they can be paid
warehouse_logistics-1.explanation: A WMS helps control the movement and storage of goods in a warehouse with full tracking.

options: Receiving goods that come in from suppliers
Delivering goods to customers
Returning damaged goods from customers to the warehouse
Writing goods off the books
warehouse_logistics-2.explanation: Inbound is the flow of goods in from suppliers; outbound is the flow out to customers.

warehouse_logistics-3.stem: After goods are received and checked, moving them to their assigned shelf location is called...
options: Putaway
Picking
Cross-docking
Dispatch
warehouse_logistics-3.explanation: Putaway is placing received goods into the right storage location.

warehouse_logistics-4.stem: Goods move from the supplier's truck straight to the customer delivery truck without long storage. What is this called?
options: Cross-docking
Safety stock
A stock count
A backorder
warehouse_logistics-4.explanation: Cross-docking moves goods from receiving to shipping without long-term storage.

warehouse_logistics-5.stem: A company hands its storage and delivery of goods to an outside logistics provider. What model is this?
options: Third-party logistics (3PL)
Cross-docking at a partner's site
Just-in-time delivery
Make-to-order production
warehouse_logistics-5.explanation: 3PL means using a third-party provider for warehousing and transport.

production_planning_mrp-1.stem: The main inputs to an MRP calculation are...
options: The MPS, bill of materials and inventory status
The sales forecast, price list and supplier catalogue
The bill of materials, machine capacity and labour cost
Purchase orders, supplier invoices and payment terms
production_planning_mrp-1.explanation: MRP uses the master production schedule (MPS), the BOM and inventory records to compute material needs.

production_planning_mrp-2.stem: What is a bill of materials (BOM)?
options: The materials and quantities needed for one product
The sequence of machine operations needed for a product
The list of finished products currently held in stock
The purchase plan for raw materials over the next month
production_planning_mrp-2.explanation: A BOM details all materials, components and quantities needed for one finished unit.

production_planning_mrp-3.stem: Gross requirement for a component is 500 units, on-hand stock is 120 and scheduled receipts are 80. What is the net requirement?
options: 300 units
500 units
380 units
700 units
production_planning_mrp-3.explanation: Net requirement = gross - on hand - scheduled receipts = 500 - 120 - 80 = 300.

production_planning_mrp-4.stem: What does the master production schedule (MPS) state?
options: Which products are made, how many and when
Which raw materials to buy and when
How much machine capacity each shift has available
The sales target for each region
production_planning_mrp-4.explanation: The MPS sets the quantity and timing of finished products, which MRP then breaks into material needs.

production_planning_mrp-5.stem: Material is needed on 30 June and the supplier lead time is 10 days. By when must the order be released?
options: 20 June
10 June
30 June
9 July
production_planning_mrp-5.explanation: Order release date = due date - lead time = 30 June - 10 days = 20 June.

project_planning_wbs-1.stem: What is a work breakdown structure (WBS)?
options: Splitting project deliverables into manageable parts
A sequence of project activities with their dates
A chart of who reports to whom in the project
A list of project risks together with their owners and actions
project_planning_wbs-1.explanation: A WBS breaks the whole project scope down hierarchically into smaller components.

project_planning_wbs-2.stem: The lowest level of a WBS, used for estimating and assignment, is called a...
options: Work package
Milestone
Baseline
Charter
project_planning_wbs-2.explanation: A work package is the smallest unit in the WBS that can be estimated, scheduled and assigned.

project_planning_wbs-3.stem: What does the 100% rule for a WBS say?
options: The WBS must cover all of the project scope, no less and no more
Each work package must be assigned to a single person
The WBS must be signed off by the sponsor before any estimating starts
Each level must break the work into equal parts
project_planning_wbs-3.explanation: The 100% rule: all project work must be covered by the WBS, with no work outside the scope.

project_planning_wbs-4.stem: Which WBS element is oriented to a deliverable?
options: Sales report module
Weekly team meeting
Waiting for client approval
Daily discussion
project_planning_wbs-4.explanation: A WBS is built on deliverables (what is produced), not routine activities such as meetings.

project_planning_wbs-5.stem: The main benefit of a WBS for a project coordinator is...
options: A basis for estimating, scheduling and assigning responsibility
A list of activities in order, each with its duration and start date
A record of the decisions made in project meetings
A way to track the project's actual spending
project_planning_wbs-5.explanation: A WBS is the basis for cost and time estimates, scheduling and assigning responsibility.

project_scheduling-1.stem: What does a Gantt chart show?
options: Project activities as bars on a timeline
Dependencies between activities as a network of nodes
The breakdown of deliverables into work packages
Planned versus actual project cost over time
project_scheduling-1.explanation: A Gantt chart shows activities, their durations and timing as bars on a time axis.

options: The longest activity chain, which sets the minimum duration
The activities that cost the most money
The activities that carry the greatest risk of slipping the schedule
The activities done by the project manager
project_scheduling-2.explanation: The critical path is the longest sequence of activities; delaying it delays the whole project.

project_scheduling-3.stem: Activity A (2 days) is followed by B (3 days) and C (4 days) in parallel, then D (1 day) after both finish. What is the minimum project duration?
options: 7 days
10 days
6 days
8 days
project_scheduling-3.explanation: Path A-C-D = 2 + 4 + 1 = 7 days is longer than A-B-D = 6 days, so the minimum duration is 7 days.

project_scheduling-4.stem: What is the float (slack) of an activity on the critical path?
options: Zero days
Five days
Its own duration
Unlimited
project_scheduling-4.explanation: Activities on the critical path have no slack: their float is zero.

project_scheduling-5.stem: An activity on the critical path is 2 days late and there is no crashing. What is the effect?
options: The whole project slips by 2 days
No effect
The project slips by 1 day
The project finishes earlier than planned
project_scheduling-5.explanation: A delay on the critical path shifts the project end date by the amount of the delay.

options: Added project scope without formal control
A gradual cut in the budget
A faster schedule at no extra cost to the client
A change of team members
project_risk_change-1.explanation: Scope creep is work growing beyond the original plan without adjusting schedule and cost.

project_risk_change-2.stem: What is a change request used for?
options: Managing scope changes formally
Recording issues that have already happened
Reporting weekly progress to the project sponsor
Logging the hours worked by each team member
project_risk_change-2.explanation: A change request records a requested change so its impact is assessed and approved before work starts.

project_risk_change-3.stem: What is the first step when a change request arrives from a client?
options: Assess the impact on scope, schedule and cost
Start working on it right away
Reject it without reading
Change the budget and schedule without telling the client
project_risk_change-3.explanation: The impact is assessed first so the decision to accept or reject rests on numbers.

project_risk_change-4.stem: What does RAID stand for in a project log?
options: Risks, Assumptions, Issues, Dependencies
Reports, Approvals, Invoices, Deliverables
Resources, Allocation, Income, Deadlines
Requests, Actions, Interviews, Decisions
project_risk_change-4.explanation: A RAID log records a project's risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies in one place.

project_risk_change-5.stem: Mid-project the client asks for an extra feature while budget and schedule stay fixed. What is the best response?
options: Raise a change request and get approval before working
Do it quietly to please the client
Refuse it because the scope has already been signed off
Start the work and tell them afterwards
project_risk_change-5.explanation: An extra feature should go through change control so schedule and cost are adjusted and approved.

product_roadmap_prioritization-1.stem: What is the purpose of a product roadmap?
options: To show product direction and priorities over time
To list every planned feature with its exact release date
To record the tasks planned for each sprint
To track the bugs that users have reported
product_roadmap_prioritization-1.explanation: A roadmap communicates goals, priorities and the order of product development to the team and stakeholders.

product_roadmap_prioritization-2.stem: The letters in the MoSCoW prioritisation method stand for...
options: Must, Should, Could, Won't
Make, Ship, Check, Own
Most, Some, Chosen, Waived
Maybe, Soon, Core, Optional
product_roadmap_prioritization-2.explanation: MoSCoW sorts requirements into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have (this time).

product_roadmap_prioritization-3.stem: How is a RICE score calculated?
options: (Reach x Impact x Confidence) / Effort
(Revenue + Impact + Cost) / Effort
Reach + Impact + Confidence + Effort
Effort / (Reach x Impact)
product_roadmap_prioritization-3.explanation: RICE = (reach x impact x confidence) divided by effort; the higher the score, the higher the priority.

product_roadmap_prioritization-4.stem: Feature X: reach 2,000 users, impact 2, confidence 80%, effort 4 person-months. What is its RICE score?

product_roadmap_prioritization-5.stem: Why is a roadmap built on themes or outcomes more flexible than a feature list with dates?
options: The direction stays clear while features adapt to new priorities
Themes are easier to estimate in hours than single features
The team can commit to more features in each quarter
Stakeholders no longer need to review it each quarter
product_roadmap_prioritization-5.explanation: Themes and outcomes keep the strategic direction without tying the team to features and dates that may change.

project_tools_workspace-1.stem: What is the basic structure of a Trello board?
options: A board holds lists and lists hold cards
Folders hold spreadsheets and spreadsheets hold rows
A table holds rows and each row holds columns
A calendar holds weeks and weeks hold events
project_tools_workspace-1.explanation: In Trello, a board holds several lists and each list holds task cards.

project_tools_workspace-2.stem: On a kanban board, what does each column represent?
options: A stage of work, such as To Do, Doing, Done
A team member who is responsible for the cards in it
A month of the year when work is due
A type of budget used by the project
project_tools_workspace-2.explanation: Kanban columns show workflow stages and cards move from left to right.

project_tools_workspace-3.stem: Which card feature breaks one task into small steps?
options: A checklist
A cover
A colour sleeve
A comment
project_tools_workspace-3.explanation: A checklist splits one card into sub-tasks that can be ticked off one by one.

project_tools_workspace-4.stem: What is a due date used for on a task card?
options: Marking when the task must be done
Deciding who does the task
Storing attachments for the task
Sorting cards by priority automatically
project_tools_workspace-4.explanation: A due date shows a task's deadline so lateness is easy to see.

project_tools_workspace-5.stem: On a kanban board the 'Review' column piles up 15 cards while the other columns are empty. What does this mean?
options: There is a bottleneck in the review stage to address
Work is flowing smoothly and evenly through every stage
Every task on the board is already finished
The board columns were set up the wrong way
project_tools_workspace-5.explanation: A pile-up in one column signals a bottleneck at that stage.

options: Planning how changes reach users
Fixing defects that users report in production
Managing changes to the agreed project scope
Approving test results before the system goes live
release_delivery_management-1.explanation: Release management controls how and when product or system changes are launched.

options: A summary of the changes and fixes in the release
The test cases that were run for the release
The plan for returning to the old version if needed
The list of users who will receive access
release_delivery_management-2.explanation: Release notes tell users what is new, changed and fixed.

release_delivery_management-3.stem: What should be in place before a new system goes live?
options: Business owner sign-off of the UAT results
Developer confirmation that the code compiles
A marketing announcement sent to all users
A data backup taken after the system goes live
release_delivery_management-3.explanation: Before go-live, the user acceptance test results should be signed off by the business owner.

release_delivery_management-4.stem: What is a rollback plan for?
options: Returning to the previous version if a release goes wrong
Releasing a new feature to a small group of users before everyone
Moving data from the old system into the new one
Scheduling the release outside business hours
release_delivery_management-4.explanation: A rollback plan sets out the steps to return to the earlier state if a release fails.

release_delivery_management-5.stem: The old system is switched off at the weekend and its data moved to a new system used from Monday. This transition is called...
options: A cutover
Backlog grooming
A retrospective
Estimation
release_delivery_management-5.explanation: A cutover is the scheduled switch from the old system to the new one, including data migration.
